Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Brain Economy-Aligned
Graph Transformer

Teaching graph attention to account for the balance between the anatomical cost of a brain connection and its contribution to network communication.

Stefano Vannoni · Inês Won Sampaio · Eleonora Maggioni · Islem Rekik

Explore the code on GitHub ↗
BGT-ESREBrain connectomicsGraph representation learning

The idea

Brain connections balance wiring cost with communication value. BGT-ESRE brings this principle into a Graph Transformer: each connection’s economy directly shapes how two brain regions attend to one another, giving the model a biologically motivated way to learn from brain networks.

Brain economy, built into attention.

THE METHOD / THREE STEPS
01 / WEIGHT

Represent the trade-off

Connectivity strength is weighted by an exponential penalty on anatomical distance. This creates an economy-aligned graph in which strong, shorter connections carry more weight.

02 / MAP

Construct the ecospace

Each connection receives a two-dimensional coordinate, calculated from a pair of graph communication measures. These coordinates describe its role in the economy-aligned network.

03 / ATTEND

Rotate the interaction

EcoSpace Rotary Encoding uses those coordinates to rotate query and key vectors in opposite directions. Connection economy therefore enters the attention computation itself, shaping the representations learned for classification.

WHAT EMERGED

A useful prior for
brain graph learning.

BGT-ESRE achieved the highest mean AUC among the nine evaluated methods across three datasets: sex classification in HCP-YA, and autism classification using functional and morphological connectivity in ABIDE I.

Ablation experiments supported the contribution of both economy-aligned graph construction and rotary encoding. The strongest ecospace configurations combined measures of local segregation and global integration.

Results were evaluated with five-fold cross-validation. Anatomical distance is a proxy for wiring cost; learned attention patterns offer hypotheses about brain organisation, rather than evidence of causal mechanisms.
